name: Fit-focused dressing for body type (shoulder-to-waist illusion)

lead: Fit-focused dressing means picking cuts and tailoring that emphasise wide shoulders and a narrower waist, so your torso reads as a V-taper the moment you put the clothes on.

Fit and tailoring change where garments sit and how much volume they add, which shifts the apparent shoulder-to-waist proportion. Body-shape literature links wide shoulders and a lower waist-to-chest ratio in men with perceived attractiveness; no trial has tested specific clothing cuts for this.

paras: People look for structured shoulders, jackets and shirts that follow the waist rather than hang boxy, and tailoring that takes in extra fabric at the midsection. It is often paired with training that builds the shoulders and back. The effect shows as soon as the clothes are worn.
No health risks are documented for ordinary clothing choices. Off-the-rack sizing varies, and tailoring adds cost.

angle.text: Garment cuts that broaden the shoulders and take in the waist make your torso read as a V-taper as soon as you wear them. The change is visible on the spot, and wide shoulders with a narrow waist are linked in the body-shape literature to perceived attractiveness.

lead: Fit-focused dressing means choosing and tailoring clothes to emphasise a V-shaped torso, with broad shoulders tapering to a narrower waist, and to minimise features a wearer sees as flaws. Clothing that follows the shoulder line and takes in fabric at the waist makes the shoulder-to-waist contrast look larger, which is how people use it to look more athletic and proportioned without changing their body.[1][1]

The V shape, called the inverted triangle, is one of the described male body shapes: wider shoulders and chest, a narrow waist and a broad upper body.[1] Wikipedia notes that men commonly have wider shoulders and latissimus dorsi that give the torso this shape, and that waist-to-chest ratio in men has been studied for appeal to women.[1]

Research on attractiveness has examined body proportions rather than clothing. In 2023, Pazhoohi, Garza and Kingstone reported across four studies with 659 heterosexual women that men with larger shoulder-to-hip ratios, and taller men, were rated as more attractive, masculine and capable fighters.[2] No published trial was found testing whether particular garment cuts change how attractive a man is rated.
infobox: Emphasise a V-taper; de-emphasise perceived frame flaws

paras: Body shape is shaped by skeletal structure and by muscle and fat distribution; skeletal structure stops growing in the teen years while muscle and fat can change.[1] Men's shapes are commonly described as inverted triangle, rectangle or apple.[1] The article describes android fat distribution in men, in which fat sits in the trunk and upper body, and says testosterone supports muscle growth, with shoulder widening and ribcage expansion occurring in puberty.[1]

Practitioners describe tailoring and fit choices intended to make shoulders look broader relative to the waist. Garment sizing in general is based on chest, waist and hip measurements, and posture affects those measurements.[1]

Wikipedia's article on tailors says a bespoke suit involves a skeleton fitting in which the partly made garment is adjusted, and that nearly 75 percent of the stitching of a custom-tailored suit is still done by hand.[3] It defines a tailor as someone who makes or alters clothing, especially men's clothing.[3]

On T Nation, posters with muscular builds describe the problem fit-focused dressing addresses. One writes that even athletic or tailored-fit dress shirts have too much fabric around the waist and that off-the-rack suits cut to fit the chest and shoulders are too boxy, so they had their suits tailored to fit.[4] Another says they want an athletic cut, meaning v-tapered, and finds suits problematic.[5] A third says they cannot find a tailor willing to remove enough material for a drastic v-taper.[6]

Pazhoohi and colleagues' 2023 Archives of Sexual Behavior paper tested height and shoulder-to-hip ratio together and found a height by ratio interaction only when both varied and stimuli were realistic enough, such as silhouettes versus rendered figures.[2] A 2023 EEG study by Pazhoohi, Arantes, Kingstone and Pinal found that participants rated larger shoulder-to-hip ratios as more attractive regardless of the sex of stimulus or participant.[2]

A 2021 study by Garza and Byrd-Craven in 130 women found that those with a stronger short-term mating orientation were more attracted to men with low waist-to-chest ratios, and that women who saw themselves as attractive rated low-ratio men higher.[2] Wikipedia also cites Singh (2007), who argued that body shape reflects hormone levels during puberty.[1]
No studies found testing clothing fit or tailoring as an intervention. Related research on body proportions and perceived attractiveness exists, but it concerns bodies rather than clothing.[2]

lore.intro: In T Nation threads, lifters discuss how their trained shoulders and narrow waists fit poorly in off-the-rack shirts and suits, and trade views on tailoring.[4][5][6]

claims.claim: Tailoring is needed to show a V-taper in dress clothes
A broad-shouldered, narrow-waisted silhouette is more attractive
